report:
## Conclusion

The evidence offers **modest, preliminary support** for the claim, but it is not strong or definitive.

The best-designed study, a randomized controlled trial by Manber et al. (150 pregnant women with major depressive disorder), found that depression-specific acupuncture produced a significantly higher response rate (63%) than control acupuncture or massage combined (44%), suggesting a specific benefit beyond generic acupuncture or touch therapy (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/10.1097/aog.0b013e3181cc0816~acupuncture-for-depression-during-pregnancy-a-randomized). This remains the most rigorous trial specifically on antenatal (as opposed to postpartum) depression, and it is still frequently cited as the primary evidence base, with later protocols (e.g., the AcuAnteDep trial) explicitly designed to build on and confirm these "preliminary" findings, noting that "additional research is required" (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-016-1204-9).

Broader reviews of acupuncture for depression generally (not pregnancy-specific) are mixed: Cochrane's evaluation found insufficient high-quality evidence to draw firm conclusions about acupuncture's effectiveness for depression (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD004046_acupuncture-depression), and for the related condition of postpartum depression, systematic reviews report "conflicting evidence" and low reliability of existing meta-analyses (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9329701/).

**Bottom line:** One well-conducted RCT shows acupuncture tailored for depression can reduce symptoms in pregnant women more than control treatments, but the overall body of evidence remains limited, with only one dedicated high-quality trial and no confirmed large-scale replication, plus broader Cochrane-level skepticism about acupuncture for depression generally. The claim is plausible but should be considered "promising but unproven," not conclusively established.
